lead: The smell that defines the Fallas of Valencia. Fluffy inside, crunchy outside, rolled in sugar and served with hot chocolate. The most Valencian sweet, born of the first bonfires of the 19th century.

The pumpkin fritter is the only sweet that Valencia has turned into the symbol of an entire festival. During the Fallas — from 1 to 19 March — the whole city smells of hot oil and fried pumpkin. The fritter stalls become meeting points, obligatory stops, the perfect excuse to stay chatting beside the bonfire with a paper cone in one hand and a cup of hot chocolate in the other.

The recipe is simple but has its secrets. Orange blossom water and orange zest are the aromas that set the Valencian fritter apart from any other. Fresh yeast guarantees that fluffy interior texture. And the pumpkin — preferably from the Valencian huerta, from Vilamarxant if possible — gives the orange colour and the natural sweetness that makes it very hard to stop once you have tried one.

items.title: Bunyol de Carabassa · The Sweet of the Fallas
items.subtitle: Pumpkin fritter · Hole in the middle · Paper cone · With hot chocolate
items.body: The pumpkin fritter — bunyol de carabassa in Valencian — is the most Fallas-related dessert in Valencian gastronomy. It is impossible to imagine the Fallas without the smell of hot oil, without the paper cones full of freshly fried fritters and without the thick chocolate that goes with them. They are fluffy inside, slightly crunchy outside, sweet and orange thanks to the pumpkin of the Valencian huerta. Their ring shape with a hole in the middle is characteristic and unmistakable: that “foraet” (hole) comes from the way the fritter-maker takes the dough with fingers greased in oil and lets it drop into the hot oil. They are eaten freshly made, rolled in sugar, in a paper cone, while the city burns in Fallas. But also 365 days a year in the fritter shops and chocolate houses with the longest history in Valencia.
facts: Main season: Fallas (1–19 March) · Also: All Saints’ Day, Christmas and all year round in fritter shops

items.title: The Buñoleras · The Pioneers of the Fallas Sweet
items.subtitle: 19th c. · The carpenters’ guild · Iron drums · Wind fritters
items.body: The history of the pumpkin fritter begins in the 19th century, when the carpenters’ guild of Valencia obtained permission from the City Council to take their leftover wood out into the street and burn it in bonfires on Saint Joseph’s Day. That was the origin of the Fallas. Around those first bonfires, the carpenters’ wives — the first buñoleras, described as “neatly coiffed, very tidy and with spotless white aprons” — set up iron drums as stoves, heated oil with firewood and prepared wind fritters for those attending. Those first fritters followed an old, simple recipe: flour, water, yeast and salt, fried in oil. The neighbours had them with anisette or aguardiente, not with chocolate. Years later, the farmers of the huerta began to add seasonal pumpkin — which keeps for months in storage — to give the fritter a sweeter touch. And so was born the bunyol de carabassa we know today.
facts: Origin: 19th century · First fritter-maker: carpenters’ guild of Valencia · First with anisette, later with chocolate

items.title: The Recipe · Pumpkin, Orange and Orange Blossom Water
items.subtitle: Cooked pumpkin · Baker’s yeast · Orange zest · Orange blossom water · Frying oil
items.body: The dough of Valencian pumpkin fritters is simple but aromatic. The pumpkin is cooked until tender, drained and mashed with a fork to a smooth purée. To that paste are added the sugar, the orange blossom water and the orange zest — the most Valencian aromas there are —, the fresh yeast dissolved in the cooking water (which keeps its nutrients), and finally the sifted flour. The resulting dough should rest for about 15 minutes so the yeast can do its work. For frying, the fingers are greased in oil so the dough does not stick, a portion is taken, shaped into a ball and the central hole is made with the thumb before dropping it into the very hot oil. They are browned on both sides, drained and rolled in sugar straight away. They are served hot, in a paper cone.
facts: For 7 pieces: 200 g pumpkin · 225 g flour · 12 g fresh yeast · orange blossom water · orange zest · sugar

items.title: The Hole · The Art of the Foraet
items.subtitle: The characteristic shape · Fingers greased in oil · The fritter-maker’s technique
items.body: The central hole — the “foraet” — is the hallmark of the Valencian fritter. It is not just an aesthetic detail: it has a technical reason. By sinking the thumb into the centre of the dough before submerging it in the oil, the frying is more even and the inside is fluffier. The technique seems simple but has its art: the fingers must be well greased in oil so the dough does not stick, the ball must be exactly the right size for correct cooking, and the hole must be made decisively so it keeps its shape during frying. The oil must be very hot but not scorching — if it smokes, the fritter browns outside before cooking inside. This gesture — dough in the hand, hole, oil — is what makes the fritter-maker a craftsman. At the street stalls during the Fallas, the fritter-makers produce hundreds an hour with a skill that only practice gives.
facts: Very hot oil · Greased fingers · Central hole made with the thumb · Brown on both sides · Roll in sugar while hot

items.title: Variations · Beyond the Pumpkin
items.subtitle: Orange · Sweet potato · Fig · Horchata · Vanilla · Classic wind fritters
items.body: The pumpkin recipe is the star, but the world of Valencian fritters has many variations. Orange fritters use the citric acid of the fruit — which repels oil — to achieve a lighter fritter. Sweet potato ones are an autumn alternative with a sweeter, earthier flavour. Fig ones are the most aromatic. The horchata ones are the most Valencian innovation possible: tiger-nut milk in the dough. And the classic wind fritters — without pumpkin — are the 19th-century originals: flour, water, yeast and salt, crunchy and light, with a Roman tradition that reaches our days. The more modern versions include white or dark chocolate coatings. There are also recipes that add cinnamon, vanilla, cardamom or cloves to personalise the sweet.
facts: Variations: orange · sweet potato · fig · horchata · vanilla · classic wind · New: with chocolate coating

items.title: Pumpkin cooking water
items.body: Use the water the pumpkin was cooked in to dissolve the yeast — it has more nutrients and flavour

items.title: The 15-minute rest
items.body: Letting the dough rest covered is key — the yeast works and the fritter turns out fluffier

items.title: Fingers well greased in oil
items.body: Without oil on the fingers the dough sticks and the fritter loses its shape before it hits the oil

items.title: Very hot oil
items.body: The oil should be hot but not smoking — if it smokes, the outside burns before the inside cooks

items.title: Roll in sugar while hot
items.body: Sugar sticks much better when the fritter is hot — do not wait for it to cool

items.title: Eat them freshly made
items.body: The fritter is best freshly fried — if any are left over, keep them in an airtight container so they do not lose their texture

blocks.title: What you should know about Valencian fritters
items: Hot chocolate is the obligatory accompaniment — thick, not runny, for dipping the fritter
During the Fallas (1–19 March) street stalls serve them all day in paper cones all over Valencia
Pumpkin from Vilamarxant is the most prized for Valencian fritters — its natural sweetness is incomparable
Buñolería El Contraste (Ruzafa) is the only one that makes them all year round — five generations of tradition
The central hole is not decorative — it guarantees more even frying and a fluffier interior
You can also find them all year round on All Saints’ Day and at Christmas — not only at the Fallas
